column2: Why is more training work not automatically better for adaptation?
column3: Adaptation depends on the balance between the training signal and recoverable cost; the stimulus must exceed accustomed demand, but recovery must permit remodelling.

column2: How can endurance performance improve even when maximal oxygen uptake changes little?
column3: Performance also improves through economy, threshold, glycogen preservation, and fatigue resistance, which do not depend on maximal oxygen uptake alone.

column3: Work interval, recovery, number, mode, and intensity each change the session, so the same label covers physiologically different stimuli.

column2: What mainly explains the early strength gains of resistance training before much hypertrophy occurs?
column3: Neural adaptations: better motor-unit recruitment, firing, coordination, and skill. Hypertrophy follows later as repeated synthesis exceeds breakdown.

column2: Why does unaccustomed eccentric exercise cause more muscle damage, and what happens with repeated exposure?
column3: Eccentric contractions produce high force at lower metabolic cost, causing greater initial damage when unfamiliar; repeated exposure produces a protective repeated-bout effect.

column2: Why can rapid strength gains outpace connective-tissue readiness?
column3: Tendons adapt to repeated high tension through matrix turnover and stiffness change on a timescale that may lag muscle, so force capacity can rise before tendons are ready.

column3: It may temporarily reduce power output, whereas dynamic preparation raises temperature and rehearses the movement.

column3: Practising only when fresh may not prepare performance under realistic demand, but practising complex high-risk skills when severely fatigued can reinforce unsafe patterns.

column2: Is interference between concurrent endurance and resistance training an absolute molecular prohibition? How should it be managed?
column3: No; it depends on total load, modality, nutrition, training status, and session proximity. Place the priority quality when fatigue is lowest and allow enough recovery for its adaptation.

column2: Why is monitoring only external or only internal training load misleading?
column3: The same external load creates different internal stress with heat, illness, sleep loss, altitude, or improved fitness, so one alone can mistake declining capacity for increased effort or fitness for undertraining.

column3: Functional overreaching is a short, planned performance dip followed by improvement after recovery; nonfunctional overreaching causes longer impairment without compensating gain.

column3: It reflects structural disturbance and inflammatory sensitisation, not retained lactate, and it correlates poorly with the quality of adaptation.

column3: Different systems recover on different timescales, so heart rate may normalise while glycogen remains low, or soreness may persist after force returns.

column2: After excluding serious pathology, why are neither complete rest nor forced training the right response to an injury?
column3: Complete rest reduces capacity, while forced training through escalating dysfunction can worsen injury; tolerable function should be restored progressively.
